subject: 도덕적 사실은 존재하는가
title: Whether there are moral facts at all
content: When somebody says that torturing for amusement is wrong, they appear to state a fact. The sentence behaves like one: it can be embedded in conditionals, denied, doubted, and argued about. Whether any fact corresponds to it is among the oldest disputes in philosophy, and the positions available are fewer than the literature suggests. The realist holds that such facts exist and that moral inquiry discovers them. This explains our practice directly, since we treat moral error as possible and moral progress as real, and both notions require something for our judgments to be answerable to. The cost is that these facts must be unlike any others, detectable by no instrument and yet somehow bearing on what everybody should do. The error theorist accepts that moral claims purport to state facts and denies that any such facts exist, concluding that all such claims are false. This position takes the language seriously while refusing the metaphysics, and its difficulty is practical: nobody can actually live as though moral claims were uniformly false, and the theorists who defend it do not try. A third family denies that moral claims state facts in the first place. They express attitudes, or commitments, or the acceptance of a standard, so the question of correspondence never arises. Sophisticated versions of this view recover almost everything the realist wanted, including truth and error, which makes the remaining disagreement unusually subtle. What every position must accommodate is the same body of practice. We argue, revise, condemn, and occasionally change our minds under pressure of argument, and any theory that cannot explain why those activities make sense has failed regardless of its metaphysical tidiness. That constraint has narrowed the field considerably over the past century.

subject: 직관은 증거인가
title: Whether a strong intuition counts as evidence
content: Philosophical argument leans heavily on intuitions about cases. A thought experiment is described, most readers find that a certain verdict seems obviously right, and that verdict is then treated as data that a theory must accommodate. Whether this practice is legitimate has itself become a serious question. The case for treating intuitions as evidence rests on necessity. Some starting points are required, and in moral and conceptual inquiry there is nothing more basic to appeal to. If no judgment about a case can be trusted, then no theory can be tested, and the whole enterprise collapses into stipulation. Every discipline relies on some observations it cannot independently verify. The case against points at variation. Intuitions about the same case differ across cultures, across levels of training, and even within one person depending on how the case is presented. Reordering two scenarios changes which verdict people give, and framing effects of that kind are documented extensively. A response that shifts with presentation looks like a reaction rather than a perception. A middle position sorts intuitions by type. Judgments about clear cases are far more stable than judgments about exotic ones, and philosophers rely most heavily on exactly the exotic cases where agreement is weakest. Treating the stable judgments as evidence while handling the unstable ones cautiously is defensible and considerably less convenient. What follows for practice is a demand for honesty about what an argument rests on. An argument whose conclusion depends entirely on one contested intuition has established that the conclusion follows from that intuition, which is a real result and a smaller one than it usually claims. Stating the dependence plainly lets a reader who lacks the intuition see exactly where they may resist.

subject: 귀납은 정당화되는가
title: Why we expect the future to resemble the past
content: Every prediction assumes that patterns which have held will continue to hold. The sun has risen daily, so it will rise tomorrow; bread has nourished, so it will nourish again. This reasoning underlies all knowledge that goes beyond what has been observed, and justifying it has proved impossible in a way that remains genuinely troubling. The difficulty is easily stated. Any argument that past regularities support future expectations must assume that nature is uniform. Asked why we should believe that, the only available answer is that nature has been uniform so far, which uses exactly the principle under examination. The justification is therefore circular, and no way around the circle has been generally accepted in nearly three centuries of attempts. Several responses have been offered. One denies that justification is needed, holding that inductive reasoning defines what we mean by rationality, so demanding an external warrant misunderstands the request. Another argues that if any method works, this one does, so we lose nothing by using it. A third abandons the attempt and reconstructs science as a matter of conjecture and refutation, in which theories are never confirmed but only eliminated, although critics observe that choosing among surviving theories reintroduces the problem. A related puzzle sharpens the difficulty. The same evidence supports indefinitely many incompatible generalisations, since any set of observations fits both a simple pattern and a gerrymandered one that diverges tomorrow. Nothing in the evidence itself selects between them, so our preference must come from somewhere else. What survives the whole discussion is a practical truth. We cannot stop reasoning this way, the reasoning works remarkably well, and no account of why it works has withstood examination, which is an uncomfortable position for a species that has built everything on it.

subject: 자유 의지와 결정론
title: Whether choice survives a world of causes
content: If every event is fixed by prior causes, then so is every decision, and the sense that a person could have acted otherwise appears to be an illusion. This threat to freedom has occupied philosophers for centuries, and the debate has clarified considerably even though it has not concluded. One response denies determinism, pointing to indeterminacy in the physical description of the world. This does less for freedom than it appears, since an action produced by a random event is no more under a person's control than one produced by a fixed chain. Randomness is not agency, and any account must explain why an undetermined action counts as the person's own. A second response accepts determinism and denies that freedom requires alternatives. On this reading a person acts freely when their action flows from their own desires and judgments without external compulsion, and whether they could have done otherwise in some absolute sense is beside the point. This makes freedom compatible with a fully caused world and is by far the most widely held position among philosophers. A third response insists that genuine responsibility requires the ability to do otherwise, and that a caused choice cannot supply it. Those holding this view accept the consequence that nobody is ultimately responsible, and they argue that moral practice should be revised accordingly, replacing blame with something closer to treatment. The practical stakes are considerable. Systems of punishment rest on assumptions about desert, and if those assumptions fail, the justification shifts entirely toward prevention and protection. Even those who defend the compatibility of freedom and causation acknowledge that the reasons a person had for acting are themselves the product of circumstances nobody chose, which should temper how confidently anybody assigns blame.

subject: 무의식적 태도의 책임
title: Answering for attitudes you did not know you had
content: Evidence suggests that people hold associations they would sincerely deny and that these associations affect behaviour: whose application is read carefully, whose account is believed, whose discomfort is noticed. Whether somebody is responsible for such attitudes is a genuine moral question, since the standard conditions for blame appear unmet. Responsibility usually requires control and awareness. An attitude a person did not choose, cannot detect, and would repudiate if shown seems to satisfy neither condition, so blaming them looks like blaming somebody for their height. This argument has force and it proves too much, since it would equally excuse the effects, and those effects fall on real people. Several responses narrow the gap. One distinguishes blame for having the attitude from responsibility for its consequences. Nobody chose their associations, and yet a person can be answerable for what they do, particularly once they know that such influences exist. Ignorance excuses only until the evidence is available, which is the same principle that governs every other kind of avoidable ignorance. A second response points to indirect control. Attitudes are not directly revisable, and they respond over time to what somebody reads, whom they know, and which habits they adopt, so a person who takes no such steps has made a choice of a slower kind. This treats character as something cultivated rather than found. A third response redirects attention to structures. Where the effects of such attitudes are aggregate, individual blame is a poor instrument, and the appropriate response is to design procedures that do not depend on individual reliability. Anonymising applications and structuring interviews accomplish more than exhortation does. What follows is that moral vocabulary designed for deliberate acts fits these cases badly, and forcing them into it produces either unfair blame or an excuse that nobody should accept.

subject: 말로 행위를 한다는 것
title: Sentences that do rather than describe
content: Most utterances describe something, and moral philosophy long treated description as the central function of speech. Yet a great many sentences do not describe at all. Saying that you promise is not reporting a promise; it is making one, and the same holds for naming a ship, declaring a meeting open, or accepting an offer. Because such cases are common, recognising this changed how philosophers understood speech. Yet such utterances are not true or false. They succeed or fail, and their success depends on conditions that have nothing to do with accuracy: the speaker must have the standing to perform the act, the circumstances must be appropriate, and the procedure must be carried through. A person with no authority declaring a meeting open has said the words without doing the thing, and therefore the failure is not a falsehood at all. This insight extends much further than the obvious cases. Asserting, questioning, warning, and apologising are all acts performed in speaking, and each carries its own conditions of success. Consequently grasping an utterance requires knowing what the speaker was doing with it rather than merely what the words mean, although the two can come apart completely. A remark about the temperature may be a request to close a window. Moral consequences follow directly from this. If speech is action, then some speech harms in the way that other actions harm, which reframes arguments about what may be said. Threatening, defaming, and inciting are not descriptions that happen to have bad effects, since they are moral acts performed through words. Certain arguments about free expression assume that speech merely conveys content and therefore differs categorically from conduct, and this analysis undermines the assumption without settling the question of which acts should be restricted.

subject: 모호한 말과 경계 사례
title: Words with no sharp edge
content: Almost every ordinary term admits borderline cases. A person losing hair becomes bald at no particular moment, a heap remains a heap when one grain is removed, and there is no first tall centimetre. This vagueness is universal in natural language and it generates a paradox that has resisted solution for well over two thousand years. The paradox runs by small steps. One grain is not a heap, and adding one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap, so no number of grains makes a heap. Each premise seems obviously true and the conclusion is obviously false, which means something in the reasoning must fail even though nothing in it looks wrong. One response denies the second premise, holding that there is a sharp boundary which nobody can locate. Vagueness on this view is ignorance rather than indeterminacy, and the world is precise while our knowledge is not. The position is coherent and strikes many as incredible, since it posits a specific grain whose addition creates a heap. Another response introduces degrees of truth, so that a statement can be partly true as a case approaches the boundary. This matches how such cases feel and it complicates logic considerably, since arguments valid for definite statements may fail. A third holds that vague terms have no determinate application in borderline cases, and that saying anything definite there is simply an error. The practical consequences reach into law and policy. Statutes use vague terms constantly — reasonable, substantial, serious — and courts must apply them to cases the drafters never considered. Recognising that no fact of the matter may exist changes what a judge is doing in such a case, since they are making a boundary rather than finding one.

subject: 침묵시키기와 발화의 조건
title: How somebody can be prevented from speaking while speaking
content: Being silenced usually means being prevented from speaking. A subtler form has attracted philosophical attention: somebody speaks, the words are heard, and yet the act they were attempting does not come off. Understanding this requires the recognition that speaking is doing rather than merely emitting. Consider what a refusal requires. Saying no is an act, and like other acts it depends on conditions being in place, one of which is that the audience recognises what is being done. Where a hearer does not treat a refusal as a refusal, the words were uttered and the act failed, and the speaker has been prevented from doing something without being prevented from speaking. This has been argued at length in connection with sexual consent. A related form concerns credibility. Somebody whose testimony is systematically discounted can speak freely and never be believed, so the act of informing fails while the act of talking succeeds. Since the failure occurs in the uptake rather than in the utterance, no censor is required and no one need intend the outcome, which makes this form of silencing invisible to anybody looking for a suppressor. The moral analysis matters for arguments about expression. A framework that protects only against interference will not register these failures at all, since nobody was stopped from speaking, and yet something the freedom was supposed to protect has been lost. The value of expression lies in being able to do things with words rather than in the physical act of producing them. What follows is that securing that value requires attention to the conditions of uptake as well as to the absence of restraint. Those conditions are shaped by shared assumptions about who is credible, and changing them is slower and harder than removing a legal restriction.

subject: 권위는 어떻게 정당해지는가
title: What gives anybody the right to command
content: Authority claims something remarkable: that its orders create moral duties for people who never agreed to them, and that those duties hold even where the person judges the order wrong. Explaining how anybody acquires that standing is among the central problems in moral philosophy. One tradition holds that such authority rests on agreement. This has obvious appeal, since duties we take on ourselves are the least puzzling kind. Its trouble is factual, because almost nobody has agreed to be ruled, and the substitutes offered — silent consent read from where a person lives, or what a reasonable person would accept — either prove too much or give up the appeal to real agreement. A second tradition grounds the right to command in what it achieves. A body holds rightful authority where following its orders helps people act on reasons that already apply to them, so a traffic rule binds because acting together is truly valuable and no one person can do it alone. This account explains why the right to command reaches only so far, and why it fails where the body stops doing that work. A third tradition appeals to fairness and to justice. Where everybody gains from a scheme that needs general compliance, somebody who takes the gains while refusing the burdens is using the rest unfairly. This grounds the duty in a moral relation among members rather than in anything the ruler does. Each account leaves genuine gaps, and combining them is the usual practical response. What all of them establish is that legitimacy is conditional rather than assumed. A body that fails to coordinate, fails to benefit, and rests on no agreement has no claim beyond its power to compel, which is exactly what the idea of rightful authority was meant to be distinguished from.

subject: 다수결의 한계
title: Why counting heads does not settle everything
content: Majority decision is the default procedure for collective choice, and it has genuine virtues. It treats each participant equally, it is transparent, and it produces an answer whenever one is needed. Yet nobody defends it as a general method for settling questions, and understanding the limits clarifies what the procedure is actually for. The first limit concerns what majorities can decide. A majority cannot make a false claim true, so procedural fairness supplies no reason to accept a factual conclusion reached by voting. This is obvious for questions of measurement and less obvious for the mixed questions that dominate public argument, where a factual dispute is embedded in a value dispute and the vote settles both at once. The second limit concerns minorities. A permanent majority can impose costs on a permanent minority indefinitely, and each decision is procedurally correct while the pattern is not. Constitutional constraints exist to address exactly this, removing certain matters from ordinary decision, and the objection that such constraints are undemocratic misses that they protect the conditions under which majority rule is defensible. A third limit is technical and less familiar. Where more than two options exist, the winner depends on the voting method chosen, and different reasonable methods select different winners from identical preferences. Formal results establish that no method satisfies every condition one would want, so there is no neutral procedure waiting to be adopted. What survives is a modest defence. Majority decision is a good way to settle questions where reasonable people disagree about values, where the matter must be decided somehow, and where those who lose today may win tomorrow. Outside those conditions it carries considerably less moral weight than its familiarity suggests.

subject: 음계와 조성이라는 틀
title: The scale that most Western music assumes
content: A listener raised on European music hears certain notes as belonging together and one of them as home. That sense of a tonal centre is so immediate that it feels natural, and yet it is the product of a system worked out over several centuries and by no means universal among musical traditions. The system selects seven notes from twelve and arranges them so that they stand in unequal relations to the first. Some notes feel stable, others pull toward resolution, and a melody ending anywhere but home sounds unfinished. Composers exploit this expectation constantly, delaying arrival to create tension and then supplying it, and the whole emotional grammar of a great deal of music rests on a listener who has absorbed the pattern. Its historical development was gradual. Earlier European practice used a larger family of modes with different internal arrangements, and each carried its own character, so a piece in one mode felt distinct from a piece in another. Over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries two of these came to dominate, and the rest survived mainly in folk tradition, which is why certain traditional melodies sound archaic to modern ears. The dominance was never complete. Composers from the late nineteenth century onward deliberately weakened the tonal centre, borrowing modes from folk sources, using scales built from equal steps, and eventually abandoning a centre altogether. Audiences found the results difficult precisely because the expectation had been trained so thoroughly. What the whole history demonstrates is that a musical framework is learned rather than given. Listeners in traditions using different scales hear their own systems as equally natural, and the sense that a melody has come home is a cultural achievement that each tradition builds in its members before they are old enough to notice.

subject: 재산권의 근거
title: How anything comes to be yours
content: Property claims are enforced by force and treated as basic, and yet explaining how anybody acquires an exclusive right to a piece of the world is surprisingly hard. The world was not divided at the start, so any account must explain how a unilateral act by one person generates duties for everybody else. One classical answer appeals to labour. Somebody who works on unowned material mixes their effort with it and thereby acquires it, since their labour was theirs. The argument has intuitive force and faces well known objections: it is unclear why mixing what you own with what you do not gains the second rather than losing the first, and the account gives no principled limit on how much anybody may take. Its author added a condition requiring that enough be left for others, which is rarely satisfied. A second answer appeals to convention. Property exists because a community adopts rules assigning control, and those rules are justified by what they accomplish — settled expectations, investment, and the avoidance of conflict. On this view there is no pre-political entitlement, and the question is which rules are just rather than which acquisitions were legitimate. A third answer appeals to consequences. Assigning exclusive control produces better use of resources than leaving them open, since somebody who bears the costs and gains the benefits has reason to maintain what they hold. This justifies property in general without justifying any particular distribution, which is a substantial limitation. The practical significance is considerable. If property rests on convention or on consequences, then taxation and regulation adjust the rules rather than taking what is already somebody's, and the moral objection to redistribution loses much of its force. If it rests on acquisition, that objection stands, and the historical record of how most holdings were actually acquired becomes uncomfortable.

subject: 대위법이 요구하는 것
title: Writing lines that work alone and together
content: Counterpoint is the art of combining melodic lines that each make sense independently while producing an acceptable harmony wherever they coincide. It is among the most constrained forms of musical composition, and its difficulty is the reason it has been the core of musical training for four centuries. The constraints operate simultaneously in two directions. Horizontally, each voice must have a shape a singer could follow: leaps must be prepared and answered, the range must stay within reach, and the line must have direction. Vertically, the notes sounding together at each moment must produce intervals the tradition permits, and certain motions between voices are forbidden because they weaken independence. Satisfying one dimension frequently violates the other. Parallel motion in the same interval is prohibited precisely because it makes two voices sound like one. If both move by the same distance in the same direction, the ear stops distinguishing them, and the whole point of the texture is lost. This is not an arbitrary rule but a description of what preserves the effect the form exists to produce. Teaching proceeds by species, adding one complication at a time: first note against note, then two against one, then suspensions where a note is held across a change of harmony and must resolve downward. The method dates from the eighteenth century and is still used, because the constraints are genuinely cumulative and cannot be absorbed at once. Composers who later abandoned the style continued to study it. The training develops the ability to hear several things at once and to think in independent lines rather than in blocks of harmony, and composers of every subsequent period have described that ability as the foundation of what they do, whatever they went on to write.

subject: 관현악 편성이 커진 이유
title: Why the orchestra kept growing
content: An orchestra of the mid eighteenth century might number twenty five players. A century and a half later a single work could require more than a hundred, along with instruments that had not existed before. The growth was continuous, and its causes are more varied than a simple appetite for volume. The halls came first. Concerts moved from aristocratic rooms to public halls seating a thousand or more, and a body of sound adequate in a salon disappeared in a larger space. Players had to increase in number simply to be heard, and the string sections expanded before anything else, since a single line played by twelve instruments carries where two cannot. Instrument design followed. Stronger frames, heavier strings, and greater tension allowed each instrument to produce more sound, and the addition of keys to wind instruments made them reliable across their whole range, so composers could write for them freely. Once the technical limitations were removed, the parts written became more demanding, which in turn required players of a different standard. Composers then wrote for the forces available and asked for more. Each generation added instruments to obtain colours the existing group could not supply — additional percussion, lower brass, unusual woodwinds — and works were composed that could not be performed by any smaller body. The scale itself became expressive, since a passage for a hundred players says something no smaller group can say. The growth eventually stopped. Economic constraints made very large ensembles impractical, and composers of the twentieth century turned toward smaller mixed groups where each player is individually audible. The standard orchestra remained at roughly the size it had reached, preserved by a repertoire written for exactly those forces, which is why the ensemble now performing is essentially a nineteenth century institution.

subject: 음악 축제라는 형식
title: Hearing music away from ordinary life
content: A festival concentrates performances into a limited period at a particular place, and audiences travel to attend. The form is old, appearing in religious and civic occasions across many cultures, and its modern versions retain features that reveal what the arrangement accomplishes beyond the music itself. Concentration changes attention. Somebody attending a single concert returns home to ordinary concerns; somebody spending several days hearing related work enters a different relation with it, since each performance is heard against the others. Festivals devoted to one composer, one period, or one tradition exploit this deliberately, and their programmes are constructed as arguments rather than as sequences of attractive pieces. Place matters as much as programme. Several established festivals are held in small towns reached with difficulty, and the inconvenience is not incidental. Arriving somewhere removed from ordinary life marks the occasion as separate, and the audience that has made the journey is differently disposed from one that dropped in after work. The oldest festivals were founded on exactly this reasoning. The economic structure is distinctive. A festival can assemble performers who would never gather for a single concert, rehearse work that no regular season could afford, and stage pieces requiring forces that exist nowhere permanently. Consequently a substantial part of the repertoire that is technically demanding or unusually large is heard mainly in this setting. The form has spread far beyond its origins, and popular music festivals now attract audiences of a size that classical ones never approached. What they share with the older model is the essential structure: leaving ordinary surroundings, spending an extended period among people who came for the same reason, and hearing more in a few days than a year of separate occasions would supply.

subject: 시민권은 무엇을 주는가
title: What membership in a state actually confers
content: Citizenship is treated as a status that either applies or does not, and yet what it confers varies enormously. Examining its content reveals that it bundles several quite different things together, and separating them clarifies a good deal of argument about immigration, statelessness, and rights. The first component is security of residence. A citizen cannot be expelled from the territory, and this is the protection whose absence defines the condition of the stateless person, who may be removed from anywhere and admitted nowhere. Nothing else in the bundle matters if this is missing, since every other entitlement depends on being somewhere lawfully. The second component is political participation. Citizens vote, stand for office, and hold the institutions accountable, which is what distinguishes them from residents who may hold every other right. This component carries the strongest claim to being essential, since a person governed by institutions they cannot influence stands in a relation that political philosophy has long regarded as objectionable. The third component is a set of social entitlements — access to health provision, education, and support in need — which in many states now extends to lawful residents as well. The historical trend has been to detach these from citizenship, and the trend suggests they are grounded in presence and contribution rather than in status. The fourth is diplomatic protection abroad. Separating these components explains why arguments about who should be admitted so frequently talk past one another. Somebody objecting to extending political participation may have no objection to extending medical care, and treating the bundle as indivisible forecloses arrangements that most participants would accept. Several states already unbundle it substantially, which suggests the underlying question is which entitlements attach to presence and which to membership.

subject: 녹음이 연주를 바꾼 방식
title: How recording altered the way musicians play
content: Before recording, a performance happened once and was gone. Every audience heard a different occasion, small imperfections vanished with the sound, and nobody could set two performances side by side except in memory. Recording changed all of this, and its effect on how musicians play has been considerable. The first effect was on accuracy. A recording is heard repeatedly, so a wrong note that would have slipped past in a hall becomes permanent, and players began to put accuracy first. Comparing recordings across the past century shows a steady rise in technical cleanliness and a decline in the freedoms that earlier players took with tempo and rhythm. Whether this counts as improvement is genuinely disputed among musicians. The second effect was on interpretation. Once celebrated recordings existed, students learned from them, and a single reading of a work could become the version everybody knew. Players describe how hard it is to play a famous piece without copying a record they took in before they could read music, and ways of playing that once differed by region drew together fast. Editing changed the thing itself. A recording assembled from many takes represents a performance that never happened, and the standard rose beyond what live playing can match, so audiences arrive at concerts expecting something that cannot occur. Musicians report this as a genuine pressure rather than a complaint. There have been gains too. Recording preserved players whose art would otherwise be known only in words, allowed traditions to be studied rather than merely recalled, and put an enormous body of music within reach of people who never attend a concert. What it could not preserve was the occasion, and every recording is a document of something that was made to happen once.

subject: 마이크가 바꾼 노래
title: Singing quietly to a large room
content: Before amplification, a singer had to fill a space with their own voice. This determined everything about vocal technique in every tradition performing for large audiences: the tone had to project, the breath had to support long phrases at volume, and the parts of the voice that carry over an orchestra had to be developed at the expense of others. The microphone removed the constraint entirely. A singer could produce a sound audible only at conversational distance and have it fill an auditorium, which made available an entire range of expression that projection had excluded. Breath, the catch in a voice, the sound of a consonant, and the shift into speech all became usable material, since they now reached the audience. A new style developed rapidly. Singers of the mid twentieth century worked close to the instrument, using its response to distance as a dynamic control, moving back for a loud passage and forward for an intimate one. The technique is subtle and entirely dependent on equipment, and the recordings that resulted sound as though the performer were speaking to one listener rather than addressing a crowd. Critics at the time regarded this as cheating. Reviewers accustomed to trained projection described the new singers as lacking voices, which was true by the older standard and irrelevant by the new one, since the two techniques pursue different ends. The disagreement was a genuine aesthetic dispute rather than mere conservatism. Both traditions continue. Opera and much choral singing remain unamplified and require the older technique, while nearly everything else assumes amplification, and the two produce sounds so different that audiences rarely move between them. What the change demonstrates is how completely a technical possibility can create an artistic style, since nothing in the material of song required either approach.

subject: 회중이 함께 부르는 노래
title: Music written for people who cannot sing
content: Congregational singing sets a specific problem for a composer. The performers are untrained, they have not rehearsed, their voices span a wide range of ability, and they must manage the piece on first encounter or after long intervals. Traditions that succeeded at this developed a body of craft, and examining it reveals principles that apply wherever amateurs perform. Melodic range is the first constraint. A tune spanning more than about an octave excludes a substantial portion of any congregation, so successful melodies stay within narrow bounds and place their highest note where the text carries emphasis. Leaps are limited, and those that occur outline familiar shapes that singers can find without training. Repetition does the rest of the work. Phrases return, verses share one tune, and the structure is regular enough that somebody arriving in the second verse can join. Where a tradition uses a repeated response between lines delivered by a leader, even a first time participant can take part immediately, and this arrangement appears independently across many cultures for exactly that reason. Text setting must be transparent. One note per syllable allows words to be understood and reduces the difficulty, and traditions with elaborate melisma reserve it for trained soloists. The relation between the natural stress of the words and the strong beats of the tune determines whether a congregation sings confidently or stumbles. What the whole craft accomplishes is participation rather than performance. A congregation is not an audience, the value lies in everybody producing the sound together, and a tune that a few sing beautifully while the rest fall silent has failed at its purpose however admirable it may be as music.

subject: 투표의 도덕
title: Whether you should vote, and how
content: An individual vote almost never determines an outcome. The probability of casting the decisive ballot in a large election is vanishingly small, so a person calculating whether their participation will change anything reaches a discouraging answer. Whether there is nonetheless a duty to vote, and what it requires, is a genuine moral question. The instrumental argument fails on its own terms and does not settle the matter. Several other grounds are available. One appeals to fairness: the arrangement benefits everybody and requires general participation, so declining while others bear the cost is a form of free riding. This applies whether or not any individual vote matters. Another appeals to expression, holding that voting registers a judgment and that participating is how a citizen occupies their position rather than a means to an outcome. A different question concerns how to vote rather than whether. If voting is the exercise of power over others, then casting a ballot carelessly is not merely wasteful but wrongful, since the person is helping to impose an outcome on people who must live with it. On this reasoning somebody who has not informed themselves may have a duty to abstain rather than a duty to participate, which reverses the usual conclusion. A third position holds that duties attach to the collective rather than to individuals. What matters is that the electorate as a whole be informed and participate, and no individual can secure that, so the obligation falls on institutions to make participation easy and information available. What emerges is that the familiar exhortation to vote conflates several distinct claims. Participating, participating thoughtfully, and supporting arrangements that let others participate are different obligations with different grounds, and treating them as one has made the public argument less useful than it might be.

subject: 노동요의 박자
title: Songs that set the pace of work
content: Work songs appear wherever people have performed heavy physical labour together, and their musical structure is determined by the task rather than by any aesthetic preference. Understanding the relationship explains why such songs sound as they do and why they vanished when the work changed. The rhythm matches the movement. Hauling a rope, raising a sail, hammering, or grinding each imposes a cycle, and the song places its accent where the effort falls, so singing and working become one action. A leader delivers a line while the crew recovers, and the crew answers on the beat where they pull, which is why the call and response form appears in labour traditions that had no contact with one another. Tempo therefore carries information. A song sung faster makes the work go faster, and a leader who understood the crew could adjust the pace to the task and to how tired everybody was. Sailing traditions preserved different songs for different jobs precisely because a capstan and a halyard require different cycles, and singing the wrong one made the work harder. The words mattered less. Verses were improvised, borrowed, and frequently obscene, and collectors who transcribed them found that the text varied endlessly while the rhythmic structure stayed fixed. This is the reverse of most song traditions, and it follows directly from what the form was for. The songs disappeared with the work. Mechanisation removed the need for coordinated human effort, and although the repertoire survives in performance and in recordings, it survives as music rather than as a tool. Singers who learned it from recordings frequently take tempos that no crew could have worked to, which is a small illustration of how completely the original function has been forgotten.

subject: 무곡이 지닌 사교의 기능
title: Dances that arrange who may meet whom
content: Social dance forms are not merely entertainment. They determine who touches whom, who may address whom, how long an encounter lasts, and who watches, and communities have regulated these arrangements with considerable attention. Reading a dance tradition as a social instrument explains features that appear arbitrary as choreography. Set dances circulate partners. A form in which couples progress along a line brings each dancer into contact with everybody else in turn, briefly and under observation, and the sequence is fixed so that nobody chooses. Such forms dominated European village and assembly dancing for centuries, and their structure permitted young people to meet within limits that the community could supervise. The couple dances that displaced them altered the arrangement fundamentally. A pair who dance together for a whole piece, in a closed hold, chosen by themselves, occupy a private relation within a public room, and the objections raised when such dances arrived were about exactly this rather than about the movement. Contemporary complaints are explicit and consistent across countries. Position within the room carried meaning too. Traditions specify who leads the set, where elders sit, and which dances belong to whom, so the floor is a diagram of standing within the community. Where a dance is reserved for married couples or for a particular age, participating announces a status. The forms changed as the societies did. Where supervision weakened and individual choice became the norm, dances requiring no partner at all became common, and a contemporary floor makes almost no arrangement of who relates to whom. That absence is itself a social fact, and dance historians read it exactly as they read the elaborate arrangements that preceded it.

subject: 법과 도덕의 거리
title: Whether an unjust rule is still law
content: A law may be wicked. It may command what is monstrous and forbid what is obligatory, and legal systems have produced such rules repeatedly. Whether such a rule counts as law at all divides two long traditions in legal philosophy, and the disagreement is not merely verbal. One tradition holds that law and morality are separate. Whether a rule is law depends on whether it was enacted by the recognised procedure, and its moral quality is a further question. This position is defended on the ground that clarity serves criticism: calling a wicked rule law while condemning it keeps both facts in view, whereas denying that it is law obscures what actually confronts a citizen. The opposing tradition holds that a sufficiently unjust rule forfeits legal validity. The argument is that law claims authority, authority generates obligations, and nothing that requires atrocity can generate an obligation, so such a rule fails at what makes anything law. Postwar courts faced this directly when trying officials who had complied with the rules of their state, and the reasoning appeared in judgments. The practical question is what a citizen or an official should do, and neither position answers it directly. Somebody who accepts that a wicked rule is law may still refuse to apply it; somebody who denies its validity may still be punished for refusing. The disagreement concerns how to describe the situation rather than how to act in it. What both traditions agree on is more important than what divides them. Legal validity does not settle moral obligation, obedience is not automatically owed, and an official who applies an unjust rule cannot defend themselves by pointing at its provenance. Two centuries of argument have established that much, whatever remains disputed about the vocabulary.

subject: 원근법의 발명
title: A method for putting depth on a flat surface
content: Linear perspective was worked out in fifteenth century Florence, and within a generation it had transformed European painting. It supplies a procedure for constructing an image as it would appear from one fixed point, with parallel lines converging on a vanishing point and objects diminishing with distance according to a rule. Earlier painting was not incompetent. Artists had represented depth by overlapping, by placing distant things higher, and by reducing scale, and these devices work well. What perspective added was consistency, since every element in a picture could be constructed within one coherent space rather than by separate judgments, and the resulting image corresponds to what a viewer would see from a specified position. The method carried an implicit claim. A perspective picture assumes a single stationary observer with one eye at a particular point, and it presents the world as available to that viewpoint. Some historians read this as expressing an emerging conception of the individual observer, and although the connection is argued about, the geometry does encode an observer in a way that earlier conventions did not. It also produced difficulties. Strict application distorts objects near the edges of a wide image, and painters frequently cheated to avoid results that looked wrong even though they were correct. A construction that is geometrically right and visually unacceptable exposes the gap between the method and the seeing it was supposed to model. Other traditions developed different conventions and did not adopt this one, using parallel projection that keeps distant objects the same size and permits a scroll to be read across its length. Neither approach is more accurate about the world; each is accurate about a different way of looking, which is what makes perspective a cultural achievement rather than a discovery.
